claim: Across studies the WM-Raven item correlation does not reliably rise with item difficulty; flat or inverted-U curves are the usual result (Unsworth and Engle 2005 N=160; Salthouse and Pink 2008 about 1000; Smolen and Chuderski N=347 and 939, overlapping data; Burgoyne 2019, complex span and visual arrays; Dokic 2025 N=543 by item difficulty, rule tokens and latent growth models). The Dokic review calls the evidence mixed with a majority null; its study count is unknown.
agent_test: Measure our agent's pass rate against token budget on an item set graded by empirical difficulty; check whether the gain from more tokens rises, flattens or peaks with difficulty.

claim: The one clear positive item-wise result (Little 2014, 130 recruited, slope .004, t(34)=2.87, p<.01, r2=.20) needs a four-task WM composite (r=.56). With OSPAN alone (r=.36) the slope was not significant (r2=.05). It has a same-lab replication with the Standard Progressive Matrices (supplement, not read), but two later independent tests (Burgoyne 2019; Dokic 2025, N=543) were null. So: replicated inside one lab, not replicated outside.
agent_test: Caution only: a null at low overall correlation is weak evidence.

claim: The item-wise test is not a valid test of the capacity hypothesis. Formal capacity models let the item-WM correlation rise, fall or stay flat depending on sample mean capacity and the WM share of ability variance; floor and ceiling alone give an inverted U.
agent_test: Run the same item set on several model sizes; if capacity matters, the correlation peak should move with model size rather than stay fixed.

claim: Rule-token count is only a weak predictor of how strongly WM matters. Link with OSPAN by tokens 1-4: r=.342,.276,.245,.113 (Unsworth and Engle) and .25,.24,.33,.21 (Wiley et al. as cited); Little found a small interaction (beta .02). Accuracy does fall with tokens (beta -0.10).
agent_test: Code-count rules per item for our task set and test whether the count predicts failure after controlling for measured item difficulty (IRT); do not use the count as the budget rule.

claim: The claim that items needing a new rule combination drive the WM link (Wiley 2011) failed to replicate: Harrison 2015 (n=208 complete) found novel r=.36 vs repeated r=.50, z(205)=-2.29; Smolen 2015 found .223 vs .197, z(34)=1.41, p=.17.
agent_test: Compare agent failure on items with novel versus repeated rule combinations at equal tokens; expect no special penalty for novelty alone.

claim: Time pressure may moderate the WM-Gf link: Chuderski 2013 (N=890) latent r=1.0 speeded, .83 moderate, .62 unspeeded; review mean r .395/.316/.263. Colom 2015 (N=302) did not replicate the monotone drop (.89, .74, .96).
agent_test: Vary the token cap on the same items and check whether the item-difficulty profile of failures changes (hard items lost first, as in Chuderski's 17.6% vs 3.7%). Zhou 2026 (MATH-500, R1-32B) gives the expected shape: optimal budget 1.0K at Level 1 up to 7.5K at Level 5.

claim: WM training does not raise fluid intelligence: Melby-Lervag 2016, 87 publications, nonverbal g=0.05 [-0.02,0.13] with treated controls; WM gains did not predict Gf gains (beta -.01). This argues against capacity as a causal lever on Gf.
agent_test: No direct agent analogue; suggests that enlarging context or memory alone may not lift reasoning. Test: add scratch memory without changing strategy and measure at equal tokens.

claim: Attention control and process overlap are rival explanations of the WM-Gf link, so capacity is not the only account (attention-control factor found in 84.4% of 90 samples per a search summary). Difference-score measures of attention control are unreliable. In LLMs, distractor interference behaves as its own dial: hard-negative count lowers retrieval (2026 preprint) and its link to binding capacity is inconclusive (Spearman -0.473, p=.142; +0.20, p=.56, n=11).
agent_test: Test whether agent failure comes from lost information (capacity) or from distraction: add distractor text at fixed length and compare.

claim: The latent WM-Gf correlation is high (.74 to .96 in latent models) and does not depend on set size or first versus late trials (Salthouse and Pink 2008; Colom 2015), so strong WM-Gf overlap does not by itself show a load-driven mechanism.
agent_test: None direct; informs how to read any single correlation between agent memory use and score.

claim: For LLMs, entity count or input size is a poor proxy for difficulty; relational complexity (operands bound at once) predicts failure. REL (Opus 4.5, Gemini 3 Pro, GPT-5.2): accuracy falls 45% from RC 3 to 9 with entities fixed; RC explains 24/32/44% of explainable variance; fixed-RC larger inputs improved. Patil 2026: parallel branch count is a scale-invariant bottleneck (accurate to 12 branches, collapse at 20-30). Both are recent preprints.
agent_test: Code-estimate relational complexity (jointly bound items) per step; decompose (O3) when it exceeds the level at which our agent's plain accuracy drops; compare with decomposing by length. Note: Patil 2026 found the parallel-branch collapse at 20-30 for all models from 8B to 235B, so do not expect model size alone to move the threshold.

claim: Webb 2023: for GPT-3 and humans on text matrices, the number of unique rules mattered even with total rules held constant (humans OR .61; GPT-3 OR .25). So even for LLMs it is rule diversity, not rule count alone.
agent_test: Build item sets that hold total rule count fixed and vary unique rules; compare agent accuracy.

claim: In rule-based matrix benchmarks LLMs lose accuracy with load (I-RAVEN-X arithmetic: reasoning models 80.5% to 63.0%, plain LLMs 59.3% to 4.4%), but perceptual uncertainty hurts more than longer rules or wider ranges for o3-mini and R1 (cost 5.6% and a 2.2% gain).
agent_test: Separate perception errors from rule errors by giving symbolic input; measure which dominates for our agent.

claim: More test-time compute and in-context examples do not remove the high-relational-complexity failure in REL (token cap 4096 to 16384 gave about 2-3% on REL-A4/A5, 0.4% average on REL-C; in-context examples +3.4 to +6.6 points but the task ordering stayed). Lawsen 2025 disputes parts of the collapse-with-complexity story as an artefact of output limits and unsolvable puzzles (Lua function at N=15 in under 5,000 tokens). Zhou 2026 finds returns from more thinking fall and turn negative, with the best budget rising with difficulty.
agent_test: At fixed total tokens compare one long attempt with several short ones on high-RC items; log truncations to check the output-limit confound.

claim: LLM n-back accuracy falls as n rises (gpt-3.5-turbo, capacity about 3 per Gong 2024), but part of the drop is task misunderstanding: weak models answer a different m-back task, and a strong model reached 84.75-90.08% at 8 to 10-back with demonstrations (Hu and Lewis 2025).
agent_test: Before reading a drop as a capacity limit, check by code whether answers match a different task; add a comprehension check in S1.

claim: In NeuroCognition (10 LLMs), disabling reasoning raised text multiple-choice RAPM for some models (p=.021), pattern hints gave no gain, and notes helped only marginally. Two models had reasoning disabled because overthinking exhausted output limits.
agent_test: Run RAPM-style items with reasoning on, off and capped, at equal tokens.

claim: LLM performance may carry one general factor (75% of variance over 156 models, NeuroCognition) and backward digit span may track text Raven and ARC-AGI-1 in 15 models (snippet only).
agent_test: Not testable on one agent; context only.

claim: Item difficulty for models can be calibrated empirically with item response theory (1PL over 35 LLMs, RIDE 2026) rather than assumed from structure counts. Fitted difficulty matches human pairwise judgments well on GSM8K (94.2%) but less on ARC and Winogrande (about 73.5%) and LLM judges rank it poorly outside GSM8K (Easy2Hard-Bench).
agent_test: Fit a 1PL over agent variants on a task bank; use fitted difficulty to set budget (G12) and compare with rule-count budgets at equal tokens.

claim: Once the rule is found, LLM failure lies in maintaining it: WCST errors appear as failure to maintain set and perseveration, and externalised notes help (image-hard p=.052). Humans fail more at remembering.
agent_test: Test a fixed notes slot holding the current rule against none, at equal tokens.

claim: In seven models from 8B to 235B parameters, the parallel-branch working-memory demand collapses at the same 20 to 30 branches regardless of size (Patil 2026). The demand threshold did not move with parameter count, which differs from the human-style prediction that the curve peak shifts with mean capacity.
agent_test: Run the same branch-count sweep on our agent with and without a notes slot, at equal tokens, and see whether the collapse point moves.

claim: A measurable in-context binding capacity exists for open LLMs: K50 = c * N^0.82 for 12 models up to 3B (R2=.73), but the Pythia ladder stays at k 3 to 6 across 410M to 12B and pretraining recipe matters. It was measured on recall, never against reasoning item demand.
agent_test: Use binding count as the capacity axis in the Frischkorn-style sweep; do not assume parameters set it.

claim: No LLM study was found that crosses several capacity levels with item-wise demand on reasoning items (the Frischkorn and Oberauer design). Closest: Patil 2026 (size, branch demand) and Ravulapalli 2026 (size, binding recall). The search was limited by exhausted web search quota and rate-limited APIs.
agent_test: We would have to run it: at least 3 capacity levels (model or context or notes), items graded by fitted difficulty, equal tokens.

claim: Decomposing by code restores performance when the failing step is exact indexing or enumeration (GPT-4 with code reached human level on shuffled-alphabet analogies, P=.496 vs humans; Lua function solved Hanoi N=15 in under 5,000 tokens), but did not remove the decline when the model still had to hold a joint set (REL isomer task with RDKit: recall .109, .094, .079). The REL tool arm is a different model, so it is not a paired test.
agent_test: Log which step fails; send indexing or counting steps to code (O3) and keep joint-binding steps under S2 compression, at equal tokens.

claim: In a token-budget sweep, the best reasoning length rises with item difficulty (MATH-500: about 1.0K tokens at Level 1 to 7.5K at Level 5; AIME R1-32B 41.4% at 2K, 55.6% at 10K, 53.1% at 16K). A tight cap loses hard items first and a large one hurts easy items by overthinking (67.5% of 80 checked negative flips).
agent_test: Cap-by-difficulty grid on our bank; set the cap per difficulty class and compare with one global cap at equal total tokens.

claim: Structure-based difficulty predictors fall short of fitted difficulty: LLM-judged task features reached held-out AUC .74 to .84 against oracle IRT .92 to .95 and baseline .66 to .73 on four coding-agent benchmarks, and agent ability splits additively into an LLM part and a scaffold part. No study was found that pits rule count against fitted IRT on matrix items for LLMs.
agent_test: On our own bank, fit 1PL difficulty, then compare a rule-count budget with a fitted-difficulty budget at equal tokens.

claim: Carpenter, Just and Shell (1990), as described second-hand by Little 2014: number of rule tokens explained 57% of the variance in Raven item accuracy, with a rule taxonomy and two production-system models. The original and Kyllonen and Christal 1990 (latent r .80 to .88) were not opened.
agent_test: None direct; rule count predicts average accuracy but not WM load, so use it as a feature, not as the budget rule.
